note: Occupied areas and arrows are approximate; the war had no continuous front lines, so areas show who held the ground around the places fought over, not exact boundaries.
dataNote: Occupied areas and arrows are approximate reconstructions from campaign maps and the cited articles.

chapters.title: Calcutta lost and retaken; Plassey
chapters.text: In June 1756 Siraj ud-Daulah, the new Nawab of Bengal, angered by the East India Company's new fortifications, took Calcutta on 20 June. Robert Clive came by sea from Madras, retook Calcutta on 2 January 1757 and seized the French post of Chandernagore on 23 March. At Plassey on 23 June his small army beat the Nawab, whose commander Mir Jafar had been bribed to hold back; Clive entered Murshidabad on 29 June and made Mir Jafar Nawab, leaving the Company the real power in Bengal.

chapters.title: Frederick invades Saxony
arrows: Ferdinand of Brunswick's column via Leipzig
chapters.text: Expecting Austria, Russia and France to attack him, Frederick II of Prussia struck first: on 29 August 1756 three Prussian columns invaded Austria's ally Saxony, and Frederick occupied Dresden on 9 September. The Saxon army shut itself in a fortified camp at Pirna. An Austrian army marching to its rescue was stopped at Lobositz in Bohemia on 1 October, and the starving Saxons surrendered in mid-October; Prussia held and taxed Saxony for the rest of the war.

chapters.title: Prague and Kolín
arrows: Prussian invasion of Bohemia from Saxony
chapters.text: In spring 1757 Frederick invaded Bohemia from Saxony and Silesia, beat the Austrians outside Prague on 6 May and besieged the city. An Austrian army under Daun came to relieve it and defeated Frederick at Kolín on 18 June. Frederick had to give up the siege and retreat to Saxony.

chapters.title: Rossbach and Leuthen
arrows: Frederick marches against the Franco-Imperial army
Frederick's march from Saxony to Silesia
chapters.text: With enemies closing in from every side, Frederick routed a much larger French and Imperial army at Rossbach in Saxony on 5 November 1757. Meanwhile the Austrians overran Silesia, taking Schweidnitz and, on 25 November, Breslau. Frederick marched east and on 5 December smashed the Austrian army at Leuthen with a surprise flank attack; Breslau surrendered on 19–20 December, though Schweidnitz held out until the spring.

chapters.title: Lally's offensive and the siege of Madras
chapters.text: The Comte de Lally reached Pondicherry in April 1758 with French reinforcements and within weeks took the British Fort St David at Cuddalore. In December he besieged Madras: his troops took the unfortified Black Town on 14 December, but the British held out in Fort St George. When British ships arrived with reinforcements on 16 February 1759, Lally gave up the siege.

chapters.title: 1758: Louisbourg to Fort Duquesne
arrows: Abercrombie's attack on Fort Carillon, and retreat
chapters.text: After two years of French successes on the frontier, Britain sent large forces to North America. A British army landed near the French fortress of Louisbourg on 8 June 1758 and forced it to surrender on 26 July, opening the St Lawrence. The main army was thrown back at Fort Carillon (Ticonderoga) on 8 July, but a raid destroyed Fort Frontenac on Lake Ontario in August, and in November the French blew up Fort Duquesne as Forbes's army approached; the British took the site on 25 November.

chapters.title: Quebec, 1759
arrows: Wolfe's army comes up the St Lawrence
Wolfe's landing at the Anse au Foulon
chapters.text: In June 1759 a British fleet carried James Wolfe's army up the St Lawrence; it landed on the Île d'Orléans on 28 June and set up guns at Pointe-Lévy, across from Quebec. After a summer of failed attacks, Wolfe's troops climbed the cliffs at the Anse au Foulon at night and beat Montcalm's army on the Plains of Abraham on 13 September; both generals were mortally wounded. Quebec surrendered on 18 September.

chapters.title: Kunersdorf
arrows: Saltykov's Russians advance to the Oder
chapters.text: In July 1759 a Russian army beat a Prussian corps at Kay on 23 July and occupied Frankfurt an der Oder on 31 July, where Austrians joined it. Frederick attacked their camp at Kunersdorf on 12 August and suffered his worst defeat: his army was scattered and he thought the war lost. But the allies did not march on Berlin, and Frederick survived, though an Austrian and Imperial army took Dresden in early September.

chapters.title: Wandiwash and the fall of Pondicherry
chapters.text: In January 1760 Lally tried to retake the fort of Wandiwash from the British. Eyre Coote's army came up from Madras and decisively beat him there on 22 January. The British then took the French-held forts one by one, and from September besieged Pondicherry, which surrendered on 15 January 1761, ending French power in India.

chapters.title: Montreal, 1760
arrows: Murray's advance up the St Lawrence
Amherst's advance down the St Lawrence
chapters.text: In April 1760 the French under Lévis beat the British outside Quebec at Sainte-Foy on 28 April and besieged the city, but gave up when British ships arrived in May. That summer three British armies closed on Montreal: from Quebec up the river, from Lake Champlain and from Lake Ontario, taking French forts on the way. Surrounded, the governor surrendered Montreal and all of Canada on 8 September.

chapters.title: Prussia survives: the peace of Hubertusburg
chapters.text: The death of Empress Elizabeth of Russia on 5 January 1762 saved Prussia: her successor Peter III made peace on 5 May and gave back the land Russia had occupied. Frederick beat the Austrians at Burkersdorf on 21 July and retook Schweidnitz on 9 October, and his brother Henry won at Freiberg on 29 October, though Austria still held Dresden and Glatz. The Treaty of Paris (10 February 1763) ended the war overseas, and at Hubertusburg on 15 February Austria accepted that Silesia stayed Prussian.
